practical.title: Interactive Lab: Variables, Data Types, and User Input in C — Simple Calculator
practical.sourceActivity: Interactive Lab: Variables, Data Types, and User Input in C — Simple Calculator

teachingPlaylist.title: Run and Observe the Starter Calculator
teachingPlaylist.description: Compile and run calculator.c to see current behavior: it reads two integers and prints only their sum.
teachingPlaylist.learningGoal: Identify variable declarations and how scanf with & stores user input.
teachingPlaylist.narratorScript: Run the program and observe the two prompts and the single printed Sum line. Note the use of & with scanf — it's providing the address of the variable so scanf can store the input value.
teachingPlaylist.workedExample: Input 10 and 3; the program prints Sum: 13.
teachingPlaylist.scenario: You are investigating what the provided code already does before editing it.
teachingPlaylist.learnerPrompt: Run the compile and run commands. Write a one-line explanation: why is & required with scanf?
teachingPlaylist.commonMistake: Forgetting the & leads to undefined behavior or segmentation faults.
teachingPlaylist.recap: You observed scanf reading two ints and the program printing the sum.

teachingPlaylist.title: Fill the TODOs: Difference, Product, Quotient
teachingPlaylist.description: Add printf calls for difference and product, and a formatted floating-point quotient using casting.
teachingPlaylist.learningGoal: Practice arithmetic operators and type casting for float division.
teachingPlaylist.narratorScript: Add three printf lines. Use %i for integer outputs and (float) cast plus %.2f for a readable decimal quotient.
teachingPlaylist.workedExample: After edits, 10 and 3 should print Quotient: 3.33.
teachingPlaylist.scenario: You improve the calculator by implementing missing outputs.
teachingPlaylist.learnerPrompt: Edit, compile, and run with 10 and 3 to confirm outputs.
teachingPlaylist.commonMistake: Using %f without casting operands will still perform integer division first.
teachingPlaylist.recap: You added difference, product, and a correctly formatted quotient.
codeSteps: Edit calculator.c to add three printf lines.

teachingPlaylist.title: Add Safety: Division-by-Zero Guard and Remainder
teachingPlaylist.description: Introduce a check to avoid division/modulo by zero and print an informative message.
teachingPlaylist.learningGoal: Use conditionals to prevent runtime errors and print remainder when safe.
teachingPlaylist.narratorScript: Add an if (num2 == 0) branch to handle zero divisor. In else branch compute quotient and remainder safely.
teachingPlaylist.workedExample: Input 10 and 0 -> 'Cannot divide by zero.' Input 10 and 3 -> 'Remainder: 1'.
teachingPlaylist.scenario: You make the tool safe for real users by handling invalid input.
teachingPlaylist.learnerPrompt: Implement the guard and test both zero and nonzero divisor cases.
teachingPlaylist.commonMistake: Computing remainder without guarding causes crashes.
teachingPlaylist.recap: You learned to add simple guards and why they're important.
codeSteps: Edit calculator.c to add if (num2 == 0) branch.
Compile and test with 0 and nonzero divisor.

teachingPlaylist.title: Verify Edge Cases and Plan an Extension to Floats
teachingPlaylist.description: Test negative and large inputs; plan how to support floating-point input.
teachingPlaylist.learningGoal: Confirm behavior with edge-case inputs and prepare to change types for decimals.
teachingPlaylist.narratorScript: Run tests with -5 and 2 and with large numbers. To accept decimals, change ints to float/double and update scanf/printf format specifiers accordingly.
teachingPlaylist.workedExample: Input -5 and 2 produces Sum: -3 and Product: -10.
teachingPlaylist.scenario: You validate correctness and prepare to extend the program.
teachingPlaylist.learnerPrompt: Run the edge-case tests and write down the three edits needed to accept floats.
teachingPlaylist.commonMistake: Changing only format specifiers without changing variable types leads to incorrect behavior.
teachingPlaylist.recap: You verified edge cases and planned the float/double extension.
codeSteps: Plan edits: variable types, scanf formats, printf formats.

tasks.title: Scene 1 — Observe & Understand: Run the starter program
tasks.narratorGuide: Let's compile and run the starter program exactly as provided. Watch the prompts and the computed sum. As you watch, predict what will print for the input pair 10 and 3. Notice where the program uses & with scanf, and how only the sum is shown because the other operations are left as TODOs. After running, I'll ask you to explain in one sentence why the & is required and to predict what would change if %i were replaced with %f.

tasks.title: Scene 2 — Modify & Experiment: Fill in the TODOs
tasks.narratorGuide: Now make a focused change: add three printf lines beneath the existing sum line. One prints the difference with %i, one prints the product with %i, and one prints the floating-point quotient using (float)num1 / num2 formatted with %.2f. Save, compile, and run with inputs 10 and 3. Predict the printed quotient before running. This small edit teaches type casting and format specifiers with immediate feedback.

tasks.title: Scene 3 — Build & Integrate: Handle division by zero + remainder
tasks.narratorGuide: Add a guard against division by zero: if num2 == 0 print a message and skip quotient/remainder computation. Otherwise compute quotient (with casting) and remainder (num1 % num2). Compile and run with inputs 10 and 0 to see the message, and with 10 and 3 to see the remainder 1. This exercise shows how small conditional checks prevent runtime errors and improve user experience.

tasks.title: Scene 4 — Verify & Extend: Edge cases and next-step extension
tasks.narratorGuide: Run tests with negative values and large integers to verify correctness. Then consider the extension: change num1 and num2 to float or double, update scanf to %f or %lf, and update printf format specifiers. If you change to float: declare float a, b; use scanf("%f", &a); printf("Sum: %.2f\n", a + b); — you'll also no longer need casting for division. Try negative inputs (-5 and 2) and large inputs to see the results.
